name: TLV75801PDRVR
title: TLV758P 500 mA adjustable low-dropout regulator with output discharge
summary: The TLV758P is a PMOS linear regulator for loads up to 500 mA, set to any output from 0.55 V to 5.5 V by two resistors on FB and run from 1.5 V to 6.0 V. Dropout is 130 mV at most at 500 mA for outputs of 3.3 V and above, ground current is 25 µA typical, and the 0.55 V reference holds ±1 % from −40 °C to 85 °C. It is stable with a 1 µF ceramic output capacitor, starts with a monotonic soft-start, and has an active-high enable, a 95 Ω output pulldown when off, undervoltage lockout, brick-wall-to-foldback current limit and thermal shutdown. It comes in a 2 mm × 2 mm 6-pin WSON (DRV) with a thermal pad and in a 5-pin SOT-23 (DBV).

circuits.title: Typical application, adjustable output
circuits.description: The regulator runs from VIN with CIN at its input and COUT at its output. R1 from OUT to FB and R2 from FB to ground set the output: VOUT = 0.55 V × (1 + R1 / R2). EN is driven by its own control line, VEN, and DNC is left open. Both capacitors must be 1 µF or more; the worked design, 3.8 V in and 3.3 V out at 500 mA, uses 2.2 µF for each.
notes: For R1 and R2, R1 + R2 ≤ VOUT / (100 × IFB) keeps the FB current error negligible.

circuits.title: Reverse-current protection with a Schottky diode
circuits.description: A Schottky diode D1 runs from OUT (anode) to IN (cathode), across the same nodes as the internal body diode of the pass transistor, as external protection against reverse current. CIN and COUT go from IN and OUT to ground.

operation.text: A bandgap reference and error amplifier drive a PMOS pass transistor between IN and OUT, with the output fed back on FB. Around the loop sit current limit, thermal shutdown, UVLO and enable logic, and a 95 Ω switch that grounds OUT when the part is off.
The output stays off until VIN passes the rising UVLO threshold (1.33 V typ). While VIN is below VUVLO the output is pulled to ground through RPULLDOWN.

EN is active high: above VEN(HI) (1.0 V min) the part runs, below VEN(LO) (0.3 V max) it shuts down. Where no shutdown is needed EN is tied to IN. When disabled, the pass transistor and internal circuits turn off and an internal MOSFET connects RPULLDOWN from OUT to ground, discharging COUT with the time constant of RPULLDOWN in parallel with the load.

The limit is brick-wall above the foldback voltage, VFOLDBACK = 0.4 × VOUT(NOM), holding the output current at ICL (720 mA typ). Below VFOLDBACK the limit folds back as the output falls toward ground, down to ISC (350 mA typ) into a short. In limit the output is not regulated; the pass transistor dissipates (VIN – VOUT) × ICL in brick-wall mode and (VIN – VOUT) × ISC in foldback. A lasting fault makes the part alternate between limiting and thermal shutdown.

The output turns off near 170 °C junction temperature and back on near 155 °C, so a sustained overload makes it cycle. Junction temperature is to be kept at 125 °C or less; running into thermal shutdown repeatedly reduces reliability, as the protection is meant for faults, not normal operation.

The output regulates when VIN exceeds VOUT(nom) + VDO, the load is under the current limit, TJ is under TSD, and EN has risen past its rising threshold without since falling below the falling threshold.

When VIN falls below VOUT(nom) + VDO with all else normal, the pass transistor is driven fully on as a switch in its triode region and the output follows the input. Transient response is then much worse and line or load steps can move the output a lot. Coming out of a steady dropout state (not during start-up), the output can overshoot briefly until the loop returns the pass transistor to its linear region. Dropout voltage scales roughly with load current, since the PMOS acts as a resistor RDS(ON), and PSRR and transient response worsen as VIN – VOUT nears dropout.

A slowly ramping input at start-up holds the regulator in dropout and the output can overshoot as it regains regulation; starting the part with EN avoids this. A line step out of dropout can also overshoot: in dropout the gate has been pulled to ground, and the error amplifier needs time to charge the gate capacitance back, during which the output rises until the load pulls it down. More input capacitance slows the step and reduces the overshoot.

Current forced from OUT to IN runs through the pass transistor's body diode and, if large, harms reliability by electromigration, heating or latch-up. It arises when a large COUT holds the output up while the input collapses at light load, when the output is biased before the input is present, or when something holds the output higher than the input; each can break the VOUT ≤ VIN + 0.3 V rating. Where reverse current is expected, external protection such as a Schottky diode from OUT to IN is needed.

The output needs at least 0.47 µF of effective capacitance for stability, and at most 220 µF is recommended. X5R or X7R ceramics are recommended for their stable value and ESR over temperature; DC bias derating grows with output voltage. An input capacitor is not needed for stability, but one from IN to GND lowers source impedance and helps PSRR, ripple at the input and load-step response; several in parallel help a source that is high-impedance over a wide band, and a larger one helps with fast large load steps or a source several inches away.
A capacitor CFF from OUT to FB improves transient response, noise and PSRR but is not needed for stability. A larger CFF lengthens start-up.
If VEN is above the minimum rising UVLO voltage, IN must sink 1 mA so the part does not turn on from a floating input.

Dissipation is about (VIN – VOUT) × IOUT, so the lowest input voltage that keeps regulation gives the least heat. Other heat sources nearby are to be avoided. In the DRV package most heat leaves through the thermal pad, which is soldered to a copper area with plated vias to inner planes. RθJA depends strongly on the board's copper area, weight and plane placement; the listed figure is for the JEDEC standard board and is for comparing packages. In the worked design (DRV, 3.8 V to 3.3 V at 0.5 A) the highest ambient that keeps TJ at 125 °C is 104.93 °C.
In steady operation input current about equals output current. During start-up it is higher by the current that charges COUT.
The IN pin is fed directly from a source with low output impedance.

Input and output capacitors sit right at the device pins; device connections use copper planes for heat, with thermal vias around the device. No thermal via goes directly under the DRV thermal pad, since a via there can draw solder away from the pad joint during reflow. In the DRV example, COUT sits at pin 1 and CIN at pin 6, with R1, R2 and CFF beside pins 2 and 3 over a ground plane.
